extracted.intended_audience: high-school and undergraduate students preparing for geometry contests / instructors teaching transformation geometry
extracted.subtask_description: Techniques and solution criteria for plane (and some spatial) geometry problems using vectors, complex numbers, isometries, similarities, and homotheties; includes constructions and problem-solving heuristics (contest/IMO-style).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove both directions for locus problems
rubrics_metrics.description: In locus problems one should not forget to prove two theorems. First, that the constructed point Q lies on the claimed circle (or sphere). Second, that every point of that circle (or sphere) is also a point of the locus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated in Problem 23: show Q lies on circle about O with specified radius by algebra/expansion, then for an arbitrary point Q on that circle construct A and B (or analogous points) to show it arises from the locus; check rectangle/orthogonality properties as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use vectors and complex numbers as transformations
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems solvable by vectors or complex numbers are usually good examples for transformation geometric methods: vectors are translations, multiplication by a complex number is a stretch from O combined with a rotation about O.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assign complex numbers/vectors to points, use algebraic identities (averages for midpoints, multiplication for rotations/scales, roots of unity for regular polygons) to compute positions and prove geometric claims (regularity, perpendicularity, lengths). Examples throughout the section (Problems 29–36, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification and fixed-point properties of isometries
rubrics_metrics.description: Isometries are one-to-one transformations preserving distance. In the plane, direct isometries are translations and rotations (sense-preserving); opposite isometries are line reflections and glide reflections (not sense-preserving).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use fixed-point counts to identify transformations: a translation has no fixed point (except the identity), a rotation has exactly one fixed point, a line reflection has a whole line of fixed points, a glide reflection typically has none. This helps determine what a composition can be.

rubrics_metrics.name: Represent isometries as compositions of line reflections
rubrics_metrics.description: Every direct isometry is the concatenation of two line reflections; an opposite isometry can be represented as a composition of one or three line reflections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this representation to build or decompose transformations: e.g., a rotation about P by angle 2φ is two reflections in lines through P making angle φ; a translation is two reflections in parallel lines. This yields geometric descriptions of directions and magnitudes (see below).

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation from two parallel reflections: direction and distance
rubrics_metrics.description: A translation is the product of two line reflections in parallel mirrors. The direction of the translation is orthogonal to the mirrors and its distance equals twice the distance between the parallel lines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this to derive translations from given reflections or to construct parallel mirrors giving a desired translation vector.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product of two half-turns equals a translation
rubrics_metrics.description: The product (composition) of two half-turns (180° rotations) about points A and B is the translation by 2·AB (vector 2→AB).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when sequences include half-turns to replace them by a translation; useful in chaining transformations to reach target point positions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prove regularity by finding a transformation mapping vertices
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove a constructed triangle (or polygon) is regular, find a sequence of transformations that moves one vertex to another and show the composite is a rotation by the appropriate angle about the candidate center; verify that the center is fixed by the composite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example E3: move N via dilatation, rotations, half-turn, stretch etc. to P and show the composed map is rotation by +60° about M; also show M is fixed under the composition. Same pattern in E1 and E4–E6.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show parallelogram via translations (composition approach)
rubrics_metrics.description: A parallelogram is generated by a translation. To prove a quadrilateral is a parallelogram, represent a mapping taking one vertex to the next as a translation (product of other transformations) and show it takes the opposite vertex to its partner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples E5 and E6: find a product of rotations/homotheties whose net effect is a translation carrying Y→W and Z→X, hence WX is parallel and equal to YZ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use homotheties and similarity centers for tangent-circle constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: To construct a circle tangent to two given circles with the line through the points of tangency passing through a given point P, consider homotheties centered at the tangency points and the similarity centers of the two given circles; AB is determined by P and a similarity center S (lying on AB ∪ OO1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If circles are noncongruent there are two similarity centers S, S1. Lines SP and S1P may intersect the circles and yield up to four solutions (positive or negative stretch factors). See E10 and Fig. 12.20 for constructive details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct perpendicular through point using ruler only (orthocenter method)
rubrics_metrics.description: With only a ruler, to draw the perpendicular to a diameter AB through a point P (arbitrary position), use constructions that produce the orthocenter of triangle ABP or reflections to obtain the symmetric point P' so that PP' is perpendicular to AB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General case: draw AP and BP, get intersection H of constructed lines AC and BD (perpendicular relations), then PH ⟂ AB (E11). For P on the circle or on AB there are special-case constructions involving choosing auxiliary point Q and using reflections and area/shear arguments to obtain the required perpendicular.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construct parallelogram from partial data via reflections and translations
rubrics_metrics.description: Given some vertices (e.g., two opposite vertices) or distances from a fixed point, construct the parallelogram by reflecting across the midpoint (half-turn), using translations, and intersecting circles from reflected centers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples E7–E9, E12: reflect the figure at the midpoint of AC to exchange vertices; translate segments; translate DC by vector E→E' etc.; reduce to constructible triangles and circle intersections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use centroids to minimize sum of squared distances
rubrics_metrics.description: For points A,B,C, set S = (A + B + C)/3. Then the function (X−A)^2 + (X−B)^2 + (X−C)^2 attains its minimum at X = S, with minimal value expressible as (A−B)^2 + (B−C)^2 + (C−A)^2 divided by 3.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply algebraic expansion to show the centroid minimizes the sum of squared distances; useful in optimization-type geometry problems (Problem 25).

rubrics_metrics.name: Translate geometric equalities into dot-product/vector conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Expand squared-distance equalities and collect terms to obtain linear conditions in dot products (e.g., (C−A)·X = (C−A)·B), which correspond to geometric loci like perpendiculars through specified points and characterize orthocenters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vector expansion to convert between algebraic equalities and geometric statements (see Problems 26–27). Choosing special substitutions (like B = A + C − B) can simplify to show X lies on perpendiculars or through known points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit roots of unity and unit roots for regular polygons
rubrics_metrics.description: When vertices of symmetric figures (regular triangles, hexagons, etc.) are conveniently placed, employ nth roots of unity (e.g., cube roots, sixth roots) in complex-number assignments to express constructed points and midpoints succinctly and deduce regularity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: use ω (third root of unity) to characterize equilateral triangles (Problem 28); use sixth roots to compute vertices and midpoints in Problem 29 and show side vectors differ by a factor ((ζ−1)/2) giving equality or rotation relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute and compare vectors for perpendicularity and regularity checks
rubrics_metrics.description: Express side or diagonal vectors as differences of point coordinates (or complex numbers) and compare them (equal up to multiplication by i or root-of-unity factors) to verify orthogonality or equal/rotated sides (regularity/isogonality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used repeatedly: compute −→pq, −→pr etc. in complex form and show relations like (q−r) = (p−r)·(root_of_unity) or (vector)·i = perpendicular vector. This gives algebraic proofs of geometric claims (many numbered problems).

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy: reduce constructions/problems to known constructible steps
rubrics_metrics.description: In construction problems, try to reduce the task to constructing triangles, circle intersections, reflections, homotheties, translations, and half-turns whose constructions are standard; reflect or translate figures to convert given constraints into circle intersections or triangle-side constructions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include transforming given constraints by reflection at the midpoint (E7), composing homotheties to turn a mapping into a half-turn (E4), or translating segments so that remaining unknowns lie on intersections of known circles (E9).
